clue.text: Heather offers article on Terry Pratchett work

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece written on another sits below it, so the article follows

parts.note: Eric is a Discworld novel by Terry Pratchett
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A bookish gift: heather presented along with a Pratchett novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is the botanical genus of heaths and heathers.

clue.text: "I remember Port Selda" (on the up-line)

indicators.note: in a down light, travelling on the up-line means the letters are read from the bottom upward, backwards

explanation.surface: A railway memory of a station named Port Selda, glimpsed from a train heading up the line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the up-line' turns PORTSELDA backwards. Edward Thomas's poem opens 'Yes. I remember Adlestrop', about a train halting at a Gloucestershire station, so the quoted words stand for the poem.
explanation.definitionFit: The words open Edward Thomas's poem about a train stopping at that small country station.

clue.text: The quest for Snow

parts.note: Snow here is the novelist C. P. Snow, whose 1934 novel has a title meaning a hunt or quest, not a hunt for snowfall

explanation.surface: An expedition sets out in search of snowy weather.
explanation.definitionFit: C. P. Snow's early novel about a scientist is titled with this word for a hunt or quest.

clue.text: Illuminating Hamilton work

explanation.surface: A note on something enlightening that Hamilton wrote.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamps burning coal gas lit Victorian homes; Patrick Hamilton's play of 1938 bears that lamp's name.

clue.text: Vague, restful " tab possibly identifies French writer

indicators.note: possibly says these words could be arranged some other way, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A hazy, relaxed browser tab might reveal a writer from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' makes the anagram of VAGUE RESTFUL TAB, all fifteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Madame Bovary was a nineteenth-century novelist from Rouen.

clue.text: Scoffer at crime by Alice Thomas Ellis

indicators.note: the scoffer is placed at, alongside and after, the crime, giving the order of the two parts

parts.note: a sin is a wrong or crime
one who scoffs food is an eater

explanation.surface: Someone sneering at criminality, as written up by a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoffer' looks like a mocker but means one who wolfs food. The definition is a work 'by' the novelist: her 1977 novel is The Sin Eater.
explanation.definitionFit: Alice Thomas Ellis's first novel takes its title from the folk figure who ate food to take on the dead's sins.

clue.text: MacDonald's princess upsets northern Eire

indicators.note: upsets says the letters are knocked over and set down in a new order

explanation.surface: A fairy-tale royal throws the north of Ireland into disorder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsets' rearranges N plus EIRE. George MacDonald's The Princess and the Goblin has a young princess of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: George MacDonald's princess in The Princess and the Goblin is called Irene.

clue.text: Welsh poet seen to rhyme "push" inaccurately

indicators.note: inaccurately says the letters are not set down as given, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Welsh versifier is said to make a sloppy rhyme on the word push.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inaccurately' rearranges RHYME plus PUSH. Emyr Humphreys was a Welsh novelist and poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Emyr Humphreys wrote verse and fiction in Wales across the twentieth century.

clue.text: Novelist friend of Lawrence presents archetypal schoolboy and another lad

parts.note: William Brown of Richmal Crompton's Just William books is the archetypal unruly schoolboy
a son is a boy, a lad

explanation.surface: A writer close to Lawrence introduces a classic schoolboy and a second boy.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Williamson, author of Tarka the Otter, was a friend of T. E. Lawrence.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Williamson corresponded with T. E. Lawrence, who was riding to visit him when he crashed.

clue.text: Part of item made by novelist

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Something crafted by a novelist, or a piece of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a work 'by' a novelist: Jane Austen's Emma.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma is Jane Austen's novel of 1815 about a meddling matchmaker.

clue.text: Odysseus heard that she played ball

definitions.text: Odysseus heard that she played ball

parts.words: Odysseus heard that she played ball
parts.note: in the Odyssey the shipwrecked hero is woken by the cries of a princess and her maids at a ball game on the shore

explanation.surface: The hero of Homer gets word that a woman joined in a game.
explanation.definitionFit: In Odyssey Book 6 the Phaeacian princess plays ball with her maids, and their shrieks wake the castaway.

clue.text: She who was featured in fiction

definitions.text: She who was featured in fiction

parts.words: She who was featured in fiction
parts.note: Rider Haggard's novel She is named for its immortal queen, 'She-who-must-be-obeyed'

explanation.surface: A woman who once appeared in a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' is the title of Rider Haggard's novel, whose heroine is called 'She-who-must-be-obeyed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rider Haggard's immortal African queen in She bears this name.

clue.text: Emperor destroys Hamelin plague

indicators.note: destroys says the word is wrecked and its letters rebuilt in another order

parts.note: the Pied Piper rid the town of Hamelin of a plague of rats

explanation.surface: A ruler wipes out the vermin that infested Hamelin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroys' rearranges RATS, the Pied Piper's Hamelin plague.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian ruler's title comes from Caesar and means a sovereign emperor.

clue.text: Two states support dynasty in earthly paradise

indicators.note: in a down clue, pieces that support another sit beneath it, so the states come after

parts.note: the Shang were an early Chinese dynasty
RI is the abbreviation for Rhode Island, and LA for Louisiana, both US states
RI is the abbreviation for Rhode Island, and LA for Louisiana, both US states

explanation.surface: A pair of nations prop up a ruling house in a heaven on earth.
explanation.walkthrough: Shangri-La is the hidden valley of James Hilton's Lost Horizon.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilton's hidden Himalayan valley became the byword for an idyllic retreat.

clue.text: A chapel for Scrooge

explanation.surface: A place of worship suitable for a miser.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hebrew 'stone of help' names many Welsh nonconformist chapels, and Dickens gave it to Scrooge as his first name.

clue.text: Foundling in strange passé epic

indicators.note: strange says the letters appear in an odd, unfamiliar order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: An abandoned child turns up in an odd, dated heroic poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges PASSE plus EPIC. In George Eliot's Silas Marner the foundling Eppie is the daughter of Godfrey Cass.
explanation.definitionFit: The golden-haired child who toddles into Silas Marner's cottage is Godfrey Cass's abandoned daughter.

clue.text: Charles Dibdin's renegade

definitions.meaning: Charles Dibdin wrote a 1770s comic opera with this title, about a soldier who runs away

explanation.surface: A turncoat belonging to the songwriter Dibdin.
explanation.definitionFit: A renegade abandons his side, as the runaway soldier in Dibdin's opera does.

clue.text: One of several Commonwealth poets said to be coming men

definitions.meaning: Thomas, Roy and Wilfred are poets from Scotland, South Africa and Canada sharing one surname
the Scottish song 'The ... Are Coming' says members of this clan are on their way

explanation.surface: A poet from the old Empire, one of a band reputed to be on the way up.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas (Scotland), Roy (South Africa) and Wilfred (Canada) share the surname; the old Scottish song is 'The Campbells Are Coming'.
explanation.definitionFit: Several Commonwealth poets share this Scottish clan name, and the song of the clan's march says its men are on their way.

clue.text: Job at Bukowski's office

definitions.meaning: Charles Bukowski's first novel, ... Office, is set in the US postal service; this word comes before office in its title

explanation.surface: Working in the place where Bukowski did his desk job.
explanation.definitionFit: A post is a position of employment, and Bukowski's 1971 novel is called Post Office.

clue.text: 12 must be

parts.note: the heroine of 12 across is known as She-who-must-be followed by a word for done as ordered

explanation.surface: Something required of the number twelve.
explanation.walkthrough: Rider Haggard's queen, answer to 12 across, is 'She-who-must-be-obeyed', so the word needed completes her title.
explanation.definitionFit: Complied with or done as told, completing the title of Haggard's imperious queen.

clue.text: Appellation given to Scipio, acquiring silver and terribly mean

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

indicators.note: terribly says the word is badly mangled, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The Roman general earns a title by gaining silver and behaving very stingily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' rearranges MEAN. 'Africanus' was the extra name, the agnomen, given to Scipio for his African victory.
explanation.definitionFit: An agname, or agnomen, is an extra Roman cognomen honouring a feat, as Africanus did for Scipio.

clue.text: He may have ruled in Hanley's 1978 subject matter

definitions.text: He may have ruled in Hanley's 1978 subject matter

parts.words: He may have ruled in Hanley's 1978 subject matter
parts.note: James Hanley's 1978 novel takes a realm as its title, and the person described is one who would have reigned over such a realm

explanation.surface: Who might have governed in the world of a late Hanley novel.
explanation.walkthrough: James Hanley's last novel (1978) is titled with the word for a monarch's realm, preceded by the article; the ruler's title, with that article, opens the book's title.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch rules over a realm, and James Hanley's 1978 novel bears that realm's name.

clue.text: Broadly embracing title of Mount's Pacific Tale

definitions.meaning: Ferdinand Mount's 1994 novel is subtitled A Pacific Tale

explanation.surface: Something wide in scope, the name of a South Seas story by Mount.
explanation.definitionFit: An overarching or all-covering term is one that shelters many things, and Ferdinand Mount's Fiji novel takes that name.

clue.text: Yeats and Eliot published such poems

definitions.text: Yeats and Eliot published such poems

parts.words: Yeats and Eliot published such poems
parts.note: both poets issued collections whose titles describe the work as coming after the earlier verse

explanation.surface: Two great modern poets brought out verse of this kind.
explanation.walkthrough: Yeats published Later Poems in 1922, and Eliot's late collected verse appeared under a similar title.
explanation.definitionFit: Subsequent, coming after the early work, as in Yeats's 1922 collection.

clue.text: US soldiers in filmed French novel

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier, and the plural supplies two of them
a GI is an American soldier, and the plural supplies two of them

explanation.surface: American troops appear in a screen adaptation of a book from France.
explanation.walkthrough: Colette's novella was made into the 1958 musical film.
explanation.definitionFit: Colette's 1944 novella about a Parisian girl was filmed as a Lerner and Loewe musical.

clue.text: Haydn tests composition a dramatic epic

indicators.note: composition means putting together, so these letters are assembled into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A Haydn work put on trial as something grand and theatrical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composition' rearranges HAYDN TESTS. Thomas Hardy's verse drama of the Napoleonic wars is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's vast verse drama of the Napoleonic wars was written for mental performance.

clue.text: Fiercely ambitious queen of a Juno sort

definitions.text: Fiercely ambitious queen of a Juno sort

parts.words: Fiercely ambitious queen of a Juno sort
parts.note: a sort, or rearrangement, of the letters of a Juno gives Anjou, so this is the ruthless queen of Henry VI, from Anjou

explanation.surface: A ruthlessly driven queen, rather like the Roman goddess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort' rearranges A JUNO into ANJOU: Henry VI's warlike queen in Shakespeare was from Anjou, and Juno, queen of the gods, suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry VI's French consort led Lancastrian armies and is the 'she-wolf of France' in Shakespeare.

clue.text: Situated by O'Neill beneath doomed trees

definitions.text: Situated by O'Neill beneath doomed trees

parts.words: Situated by O'Neill beneath doomed trees
parts.note: Eugene O'Neill's play places a certain longing under elms, trees killed off by Dutch elm disease

explanation.surface: A setting chosen by O'Neill under trees fated to die.
explanation.walkthrough: Eugene O'Neill's play is Desire Under the Elms; elms are 'doomed' by Dutch elm disease.
explanation.definitionFit: O'Neill's 1924 tragedy is titled Desire Under the Elms, placing a longing beneath those trees.
